## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension.  

Rationale  
• The statutory reform changed the maximum weekly benefit that injured workers could receive.  
• Workers with pre-injury wages above the old cap experienced a discrete jump in replacement rates, while those below the cap saw little or no change.  
• We can therefore compare high-wage (“treated”) and low-wage (“control”) claimants before vs. after the reform.  
• Because the policy was announced and implemented on a single date for the whole state, timing is arguably exogenous to the individual worker’s injury.  
• DID allows us to difference out common time shocks (macro conditions, plant closures, etc.) and permanent differences between high- and low-wage workers.  
• The event-study coefficients let us visually and formally test pre-trend similarity.

## 2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if worker’s pre-injury weekly wage (W) exceeds the pre-reform statutory cap (Cap₀); 0 otherwise.  

Control group  
Workers with W ≤ Cap₀ (they experience no or tiny change in benefits).  

Treatment timing  
Policy effective date = t₀ (e.g., 1 July 2016).  
Post = 1 for injury dates on/after t₀; 0 before.  

Alternative continuous “dose” measure  
ΔBenefitᵢ = StatutoryBenefitAfterᵢ – StatutoryBenefitBeforeᵢ  
and use it in a dose-response DID or as an instrument (see robustness).  

No RDD: running variable is not continuous around a cutoff in our preferred design, so DID is more natural.

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

1. Parallel Trends  
Absent the reform, the mean injury-duration gap between high- and low-wage claimants would have evolved similarly. Plausible because nothing else in Kentucky WC law differentially targeted high-wage workers during the sample period. We will test using pre-period event-study coefficients.

2. No Simultaneous Policies Differentially Affecting Groups  
No contemporaneous safety, health-care, or unemployment-insurance reforms that differentially hit high-wage workers. Historical review suggests none; we will cite state legislative records.

3. Stable Composition (No sorting at cutoff)  
Workers cannot perfectly time injuries to fall before/after t₀, and employers cannot reclassify wages around Cap₀ quickly. Given the unexpected nature of injuries, sorting is unlikely. We can verify by checking density of injuries around t₀ and wage distribution around Cap₀.

4. SUTVA  
One worker’s treatment status does not affect another’s injury duration. Reasonable in this context.

## 4. Threats to Identification and Remedies  

Threat 1: Differential business-cycle sensitivity (high-wage jobs may be cyclical).  
Remedy: Include firm-industry-by-year fixed effects, county-month unemployment rate controls, and test robustness in recession vs. expansion subsamples.

Threat 2: Measurement error in pre-injury wage (mis-classification into treatment).  
Remedy: Use administrative wage records if available; do robustness with ±5 % bandwidth around Cap₀ excluded (fuzzy estimation).

Threat 3: Changes in claim adjudication speed unrelated to benefit level (e.g., staffing changes).  
Remedy: Include claim examiner fixed effects, control for backlog measures, and show non-monetary claims (e.g., medical-only) are unaffected.

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# --- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)

# --- 1. Load data ----
dt <- fread("ky_wc_claims.csv")   # assume one row per claim

# --- 2. Variable construction ----
# key dates
policy_date <- as.Date("2016-07-01")

dt[, injury_date := as.Date(injury_date)]
dt[, post       := as.integer(injury_date >= policy_date)]

# Pre-reform cap (hard-code or merge statutory table)
cap0 <- 800  # example value in dollars
dt[, treated := as.integer(pre_injury_weekly_wage > cap0)]

# Outcome: duration in weeks
dt[, duration_wks := as.numeric(ceiling(absence_days/7))]

# Controls
ctrls <- c("age", "female", "tenure_yrs", "union", "firm_size", 
           "industry3", "county")

# --- 3. Main DID regression ----
did_spec <- feols(duration_wks ~ treated*post + 
                    age + female + tenure_yrs |
                    industry3 + county + year(injury_date), 
                  data = dt, cluster = ~county)

summary(did_spec)

# --- 4. Event-study (±3 years) ----
dt[, rel_quarter := as.integer( (yearquarter(injury_date) - 
                                yearquarter(policy_date)) )]

# omit -1 as baseline
event_spec <- feols(duration_wks ~ i(rel_quarter, treated, ref = -1) + 
                     age + female + tenure_yrs |
                     industry3 + county + yearquarter(injury_date), 
                   data = dt, cluster = ~county)

iplot(event_spec, xlab = "Quarter relative to reform", 
      ref.line = 0)

# --- 5. Robustness: drop injuries within ±1 month of policy ----
dt_rb <- dt[abs(injury_date - policy_date) > 30]

did_rb <- update(did_spec, data = dt_rb)
etable(list(Main = did_spec, Drop30d = did_rb),
       vcov = "cluster:county")

```

## 6. Expected Results  

Theory (moral-hazard interpretation of income replacement): Higher benefits reduce the marginal cost of not working, lengthening recovery.  
Prior: Positive effect – treated workers’ mean injury duration rises.  
Magnitude: Prior literature finds 0.1–0.2 week increase per 10 % rise in replacement rate. If the cap rise raises benefits for high-wage workers by ~15 %, expect ~1–1.5 additional weeks for those at the top.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  

C1: Parallel pre-trends       1  
C2: No other group-specific shocks  0.8  
C3: Stable composition / no sorting 0.8  
C4: Accurate treatment coding    0.7  
C5: Correct SE clustering & inference 1  

(Scale: 1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable/absent.)
